scenarios.title: Load average 32
scenarios.situation: Monitoring pages you: load average is 32 on an 8-core server. The app feels slow. A teammate says 'CPU is pegged, we need bigger machines.'
scenarios.prompt: What should you check before agreeing?
evidence: procs: r=2 b=30 | cpu: us=8 sy=4 id=10 wa=78
choices: I/O wait: 78% wa with 30 processes blocked means tasks are waiting on disk, not CPU; bigger CPUs will not help
The teammate is right; load 32 on 8 cores means the CPUs are saturated
Reboot the server to clear the load
Add more RAM, since high load always means memory pressure
scenarios.why: Load average counts runnable plus uninterruptible (usually disk-waiting) processes. The vmstat output shows CPUs 10% idle with 78% iowait: the bottleneck is storage, not compute. Bigger machines would idle faster; the fix is aimed at disk (faster volumes, fewer sync writes, query tuning).
scenarios.hint: What are those 30 blocked processes waiting for?

scenarios.title: Refused versus timeout
scenarios.situation: Your app cannot reach the database. Test A to the DB host and port returns 'connection refused' instantly. Test B to a different host hangs for 30 seconds then times out.
scenarios.prompt: What does each result tell you?
choices: Refused means you reached the host but nothing listens on that port; timeout means packets are being dropped, likely by a firewall or routing problem
Both mean the database is down; restart it
Refused is worse than timeout because the server actively rejected you
Both mean the network cable is unplugged
scenarios.why: Connection refused is an answer: your SYN reached the host and the OS replied RST because no socket is listening, so the host and route are fine and the problem is the service (down, wrong port). A timeout is silence: something between you and the target drops packets, pointing at firewalls, security groups, or routing. The fix for each is completely different.
scenarios.hint: Which result proves your packets arrived?

scenarios.title: DNS changed, nothing moved
scenarios.situation: You updated a DNS A record to point at the new server two hours ago. Half your users still reach the old server. The new server is healthy and the record is correct at the authoritative nameserver.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely explanation?
choices: TTL caching: resolvers and clients cache the old record until its time-to-live expires; the old record's TTL was long
DNS updates take 24 hours minimum to propagate worldwide
The new server is rejecting half the connections
Users need to clear their browser history
scenarios.why: DNS has no propagation: resolvers cache records for exactly the TTL you published. If the old record carried a 4-hour TTL, stragglers are expected for 4 hours. The operational lesson is to lower the TTL well before a planned migration, then raise it after. 'Propagation delay' is just TTLs expiring on their own schedule.
scenarios.hint: Who was told how long to remember the old answer?

scenarios.title: Disk full at 60%
scenarios.situation: Writes to /var fail with 'no space left on device,' but df shows the filesystem only 60% full. The application creates millions of tiny session files.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis?
choices: Inode exhaustion: the filesystem ran out of inodes (file metadata slots) from millions of tiny files, even though data blocks remain
The df output is wrong; the disk is actually full
The application needs sudo to write
The filesystem is corrupted and needs reformatting
scenarios.why: Every file consumes an inode regardless of size, and filesystems have a fixed inode count set at creation. Millions of tiny files exhaust inodes while blocks sit empty: 'no space' with free space is the signature. The fix is deleting the file sprawl (and usually consolidating sessions into fewer files), not adding disk.
scenarios.hint: What does each file consume besides its bytes?

scenarios.title: The split brain
scenarios.situation: A network partition splits your 4-node cluster into two pairs. Both sides elect themselves leader and accept writes. When the network heals, you have two divergent datasets.
scenarios.prompt: What design principle would have prevented dual leaders?
choices: Quorum: require a majority of nodes (3 of 4, ideally an odd-sized cluster) to elect a leader, so only one partition can ever hold a majority
Faster failure detection so the partition is noticed sooner
Bigger network pipes to prevent partitions
Manual leader election by the on-call engineer
scenarios.why: This is the CAP theorem in practice: during a partition you must choose consistency or availability, and quorum is how you choose consistency. With 4 nodes, a 2-2 split has no majority on either side only if you require 3; an even-sized cluster is itself the design smell, since odd sizes guarantee one side holds the majority. Detection speed and bandwidth do not change the math.
scenarios.hint: In a 2-versus-2 split, what rule lets exactly one side act?

scenarios.title: The retry storm
scenarios.situation: A payment service slows down. Clients retry aggressively on timeouts, each retry creates a new charge attempt, and the load doubles every minute until the service collapses. Customers are double-charged.
scenarios.prompt: What combination of mechanisms prevents this class of failure?
choices: Idempotency keys on charge requests plus bounded retries with exponential backoff and jitter plus circuit breakers on the client
Faster servers so timeouts never happen
Unlimited retries so every charge eventually succeeds
Disabling timeouts so clients wait as long as needed
scenarios.why: Retry storms are a feedback loop: slowness causes retries, retries cause more slowness. Idempotency keys make repeated requests safe (same key, one charge); bounded backoff with jitter spreads retry load instead of synchronizing it; circuit breakers stop clients from hammering a known-sick service. Faster servers treat the symptom; unlimited retries and no timeouts amplify the loop.
scenarios.hint: Which mechanisms make retries safe, and which make retries stop?

scenarios.title: The Systems Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Systems is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Systems?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Systems issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Systems is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Systems supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? scenarios.title: The Slow Application
scenarios.situation: Users report the app 'is slow' — pages take 8 seconds. CPU is 20%, memory 50%, disk I/O normal. The developers blame the network; network team shows clean ping. You get SSH access.
scenarios.prompt: Where do you look first, and why?
choices: Strace the app process: with CPU, memory, disk, and network all healthy, the bottleneck is likely syscall-level — lock contention (futex), excessive small I/O, or blocking on an external dependency that ping does not reveal
Add more CPU — 20% is too close to the limit
Restart the app — slow apps always need restarts
Blame the database — it is always the database
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. When all resource dashboards are green but the app is slow, the problem lives between the metrics: syscall behavior. Strace reveals lock contention (threads waiting on futex), chatty I/O (millions of tiny reads), or blocking calls to dependencies (DNS, external APIs) that ping never tests. Resource metrics measure capacity; strace measures behavior.
scenarios.hint: When dashboards are green but users suffer, what is not being measured?
objectives: Use strace to diagnose beyond resource metrics

scenarios.title: The Mystery Disk Full
scenarios.situation: Monitoring alerts: /var at 100%. df confirms. The team deletes 5GB of logs but df still shows 100%. The application keeps writing. Nobody can find what is consuming space.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause?
choices: Deleted-but-open files: the app holds file handles to deleted logs, so the kernel cannot free the blocks. Restart the app (or truncate via /proc) to release — then fix log rotation
The disk is physically failing — replace it immediately
df is wrong — trust du instead and ignore the alert
There is a hidden partition — repartition the disk
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. On Linux, deleting a file only unlinks the name; blocks free when the last handle closes. An app writing to a deleted log holds it open forever — df shows full, du cannot see the file (no name), lsof +L1 reveals it. The fix is immediate (restart/truncate) plus systemic (logrotate with copytruncate or app-level rotation). This is a top-5 Linux gotcha.
scenarios.hint: Why would df and du disagree?
objectives: Fix log rotation, not just disk space

scenarios.title: The Fork Bomb Aftermath
scenarios.situation: A runaway script fork-bombed a shared server: thousands of processes, load average 400, SSH barely responds. You finally get a shell. The system is crawling.
scenarios.prompt: What is the safe recovery sequence?
choices: Identify the parent process tree (ps --forest), kill the parent first to stop new forks, then clean up children — killing children first is futile while the parent forks faster than you kill
Kill -9 everything and reboot — fastest recovery
Wait for the OOM killer — it will sort it out
Unplug the network — isolate the damage
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A fork bomb is exponential: killing children while the parent lives is bailing with a sieve. Find the root (ppid 1's rogue child or the script's parent), SIGTERM it, then SIGKILL survivors. Prevention: ulimit -u (max user processes) in /etc/security/limits.conf — the 30-second config that makes fork bombs impossible. Recovery without prevention is a rehearsal.
scenarios.hint: Why is killing children futile while the parent lives?
objectives: Kill process trees from the parent down

scenarios.title: The Zombie Army
scenarios.situation: ps shows 200 zombie (Z state) processes. Memory and CPU are fine. A junior admin wants to kill them; a senior says 'you cannot kill zombies.' The count grows daily.
scenarios.prompt: What is the real problem and fix?
choices: Zombies are dead processes whose parents have not reaped them via wait(). The bug is in the parent process — it forks children but never collects their exit status. Fix the parent's SIGCHLD handling; killing the parent reaps all its zombies
Reboot nightly — zombies accumulate and there is no other fix
Kill -9 the zombies — SIGKILL works on everything
Ignore them — zombies use no resources so they are harmless
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. A zombie is already dead — it is just an exit code waiting to be collected. The kernel keeps it so the parent can read the status. 200 growing zombies means the parent has a wait() bug. Killing the parent orphans them to init, which reaps properly. 'Cannot kill zombies' is true (they are dead) and beside the point — fix the parent.
scenarios.hint: If the process is already dead, where is the bug?
objectives: Trace zombies to parent wait() bugs
Fix the reaper, not the reaped

scenarios.title: The Swap Death Spiral
scenarios.situation: A database server with 64GB RAM is swapping heavily. Performance collapsed. The DBA wants more RAM; the sysadmin notes the app server on the same host is using 50GB for cache. Swappiness is 60 (default).
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct intervention?
choices: The app cache is evicting database pages: set memory limits (cgroups) so the cache cannot starve the DB, lower swappiness for DB workloads (1-10), and only then evaluate if the DB genuinely needs more RAM
Add RAM immediately — swapping means insufficient memory, full stop
Disable swap entirely — swapping is always wrong
Move the database to another server — co-location was the mistake
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Swapping here is a contention problem, not a capacity problem: the app cache (reclaimable!) is pushing database pages (precious!) to disk. Cgroup limits partition memory fairly; low swappiness tells the kernel to prefer dropping file cache over swapping anonymous DB memory. Adding RAM without limits just grows the cache. Measure after limits before buying hardware.
scenarios.hint: Is this insufficient memory or unfair memory?

scenarios.title: The Permission Puzzle
scenarios.situation: A backup script running as user 'backup' cannot read /data/app/file.db. ls -l shows -rw-r----- root:appdata. User 'backup' is in group 'appdata'. The script worked yesterday. Nothing 'changed.'
scenarios.prompt: What broke?
choices: Group membership requires re-login: the backup user was added to appdata group but the running script's process started before the change — group memberships are evaluated at login/process start, not dynamically. Restart the script's session
The file permissions are wrong — chmod 777 to fix it quickly
SELinux is blocking — disable it
The disk is read-only — remount it
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Unix group membership is a login-time snapshot: existing processes keep their old group list. 'Nothing changed' is wrong — the group assignment changed, but the long-running script predates it. Fix: restart the process (new login → new groups). Verify with `id` inside the script's context vs the user's fresh shell. The 777 'fix' would work and create an audit finding.
objectives: Verify identity context, not just config

scenarios.situation: A web app spawns a thread per request. Under a traffic spike it hits 10,000 threads, then the box stops responding — not from CPU, from thread overhead.

lessons.title: Systems — Core concepts
concepts: Processes are isolated address spaces; threads share one. That single distinction explains most concurrency bugs, memory models, and why 'just add threads' often disappoints.
Virtual memory is an illusion maintained by paging: programs see contiguous addresses while the OS maps them to scattered physical pages, swapping to disk when pressured.
TCP gives you a reliable byte stream over an unreliable network via handshakes, sequence numbers, and retransmission; 'connection refused' and 'timeout' are different diagnoses with different fixes.
DNS is a caching system, not a propagation system: every answer carries a TTL, and every 'delay' is just someone's cache expiring on schedule.
Distributed systems trade via CAP: during a network partition you choose consistency or availability; quorum (majority agreement) is the standard tool for choosing consistency.
Design for partial failure: idempotency keys, bounded retries with backoff and jitter, and circuit breakers turn cascading failures into contained ones.

example.code:
$ ps -eo pid,ppid,%cpu,stat,comm --sort=-%cpu | head -5
  PID  PPID %CPU STAT COMMAND
 4182  4170 96.3 Rl   worker
 4170     1  2.1 Sl   app-server
example.walkthrough: Read the machine before theorizing: the top CPU consumer, its parent, and its state (R running, S sleeping, D disk-wait). STAT column D with high load average means disk, not CPU, no matter what the alert title says.

pitfalls: Common trap: kill -9 as the first resort; it denies the process cleanup and can corrupt state. Escalate signals gracefully.
Common trap: assuming exactly-once delivery exists; networks give at-least-once, so make operations idempotent.
Common trap: ignoring DNS TTLs before migrations, then debugging 'propagation' that is just caching.
Common trap: even-numbered clusters, which cannot form a majority during a clean 50/50 split.

lessons.title: From Static Diagrams to Living Systems
concepts: A textbook diagram shows you one part in isolation — a living systems view shows you how all parts of Acad Systems move together in sequence
The four-step systems anatomy method: (1) See the whole in context, (2) Cut it open to reveal layers, (3) Walk through the process step-by-step, (4) Pull apart into labeled pieces
Apply this to any system in this course: start with the trigger action, trace through every component it touches, watch the data flow

  → First system receives it (see the handoff)
  → Processing happens in sequence (watch each step)
  → State changes propagate (follow the ripple)
  → Final outcome delivered

Each arrow is a living handoff, not a static box.

Answering 'how does X work?' with a definition instead of walking through the sequence

lessons.title: Processes and the Scheduler
concepts: A process is a running program with its own memory space; the OS scheduler multiplexes CPU cores across processes so dozens run 'simultaneously.'
Context switches save and restore process state — they cost microseconds each, so excessive switching (thrashing) destroys throughput.
Threads share a process's memory; processes do not share. Threads are cheap to create, dangerous to synchronize. Choose by sharing needs.
Priorities and nice values bias scheduling, but the scheduler's job is fairness under load — a runaway process should not starve the system.

example.code:
SCHEDULER VIEW (ps)
  PID  %CPU  %MEM  STATE  COMMAND
  101   98    2.1   R     worker
  102    1    0.5   S     api
  103    0    0.1   Z     defunct

R=running S=sleeping Z=zombie
98% CPU on one PID → that process
is the bottleneck, not 'the server'.
example.walkthrough: Run ps/top on any machine. Identify the top CPU consumer and its state. A process at 98% R is compute-bound; many in D state means I/O wait.

pitfalls: Blaming 'the server' instead of naming the process
Creating threads without a synchronization plan — data races
Ignoring zombie processes — they signal parent bugs

lessons.title: Memory: Virtual and Real
concepts: Virtual memory gives each process its own address space; the MMU translates virtual to physical addresses transparently via page tables.
Paging moves 4KB pages between RAM and disk: page faults are normal (loading code), but major faults (disk reads) stall execution.
OOM killer sacrifices processes when memory exhausts — it chooses by badness score. Your critical service needs memory limits AND monitoring before the killer decides.
Memory leaks are allocations never freed; in managed languages, they are references never released. Profile heaps, do not guess.

example.code:
MEMORY ANATOMY
Virtual (per process): 128TB addressable
  → page tables → Physical RAM: 64GB
  → swap disk: overflow

OOM score: /proc/<pid>/oom_score
Lower it for critical services:
  echo -500 > /proc/<pid>/oom_score_adj

Leak signature: RSS grows unbounded
while workload is constant.
example.walkthrough: Check memory on a system: free -h, then find the top RSS consumers. Is growth bounded (healthy) or unbounded (leak)?

pitfalls: Confusing virtual size (VSZ) with resident (RSS) — VSZ includes mapped-but-unused
No swap and no limits: OOM killer picks victims randomly
Treating 'free memory is wasted memory' as license to ignore leaks

lessons.title: Filesystems and Storage
concepts: A filesystem maps names to blocks: inodes store metadata, directories map names to inodes, blocks hold data. Lose the inode table and names mean nothing.
Journaling filesystems (ext4, NTFS) log intended changes before applying — crash recovery replays the journal instead of full fsck.
IOPS vs throughput: databases need IOPS (many small reads), analytics need throughput (few large reads). Wrong storage type = 10x latency.
df shows space, du shows usage, inodes exhaust independently — 'disk full' with free space means inode exhaustion.

example.code:
STORAGE DIAGNOSIS
$ df -h     # space by mount
$ df -i     # inodes by mount  ← check this!
$ du -sh *  # usage by directory
$ iostat -x # IOPS, await, %util

await > 20ms → disk is the bottleneck
%util 100% + low IOPS → tiny random I/O
  (needs SSD, not bigger HDD)
example.walkthrough: Run df -h and df -i. Are inodes healthy? Then iostat: is await sane? Storage problems hide in the metric you did not check.

pitfalls: Only checking df -h and missing inode exhaustion
Putting databases on throughput-optimized storage
No filesystem monitoring — discovering full disks from users

lessons.title: System Calls: The OS Interface
concepts: System calls are the API between programs and the kernel: open, read, write, fork, exec, socket. Everything a program does with the outside world goes through syscalls.
strace shows syscalls live: run any slow program under strace to see whether it is computing, waiting on I/O, or blocked on locks.
Each syscall has a cost — crossing user/kernel boundary takes ~100ns. Programs making millions of tiny reads/writes waste time in syscall overhead; buffering exists for this.
Permissions are enforced at syscall time: the kernel checks capabilities on open(), not on read(). Open handles are the security boundary.

example.code:
STRACE A SLOW PROGRAM
$ strace -c ./myapp        # syscall summary
$ strace -e open,read ./myapp  # trace specific calls

Red flags:
  millions of read() with tiny counts
    → add buffering
  open() failing with ENOENT in a loop
    → missing file, retry storm
  futex() dominating time
    → lock contention
example.walkthrough: strace a command you use daily (with -c for summary). Which syscall dominates? Is that expected for what the program does?

pitfalls: Never using strace — debugging I/O issues by guessing

CP systems (etcd, ZooKeeper) refuse writes during partitions to stay consistent: right for coordination, locks, config. AP systems (Cassandra, Dynamo-style) keep serving and reconcile later: right for shopping carts, feeds.
Most systems are not purely one: the same product can be CP for payments and AP for recommendations. Apply CAP per subsystem, not per company.
PACELC extends CAP: even without partitions, there is a Latency vs Consistency trade-off. Every read is a choice between 'fast' and 'fresh.'

lessons.title: Consensus
concepts: Consensus = a group of machines agreeing on one value despite failures. Raft and Paxos solve it; Raft won by being understandable. Leader election + log replication is the shape.
Quorum math: with 2F+1 nodes you survive F failures (3 nodes → 1 failure, 5 → 2). Even node counts buy nothing — always odd.
Leader election is the heartbeat of consensus: followers elect a leader on timeout; the leader replicates its log. No leader, no writes — that is the CP trade-off made visible.
You almost never implement consensus: you use etcd/ZooKeeper/Consul. But you must understand it to operate them (quorum loss = write outage, split-brain prevention).

lessons.title: Replication
concepts: Synchronous replication: write confirmed on replicas before ack. Consistent, slower, and a dead replica blocks writes. For money and metadata.
Asynchronous replication: ack on primary, replicate after. Fast, with a replication-lag window where data can be lost on failover. For everything where seconds of staleness are fine.
Quorum reads/writes (R + W > N) give tunable consistency without full sync: W=2, R=2 on N=3 survives one failure with strong-ish guarantees. The knobs are the design.
Failover is the dangerous moment: promoting a lagging replica loses acknowledged writes (async) or stalls (sync). Runbooks must state the data-loss vs availability choice explicitly.

lessons.title: Partitioning and Sharding
concepts: Shard by the access pattern: user_id for user data (queries stay on one shard), time for logs (old shards go cold). The shard key determines which queries are fast and which scatter.
Hot shards: a celebrity user or giant tenant overloads one shard. Mitigations: split hot keys, composite keys, or tenant isolation. Shard keys must distribute load, not just data.
Rebalancing moves data when shards are added: consistent hashing minimizes movement. Plan rebalancing as a normal operation, not an emergency — growth is predictable.
Cross-shard transactions are the hard limit: avoid them by co-locating related data (same shard key). When unavoidable, sagas (compensating actions) beat distributed 2PC in practice.

lessons.title: Failure Detection
concepts: Heartbeats + timeouts: 'no heartbeat in T seconds = suspected dead.' T too short = false positives and flapping; T too long = slow failover. Tune to the network's actual behavior.

Split-brain: both sides of a partition think they are primary and accept writes. Fencing (STONITH — shoot the other node in the head) prevents it: the old primary must be provably dead before the new one serves.
Gossip protocols spread membership info peer-to-peer: no central point of failure, eventual convergence. How Cassandra and Consul track cluster membership.
Design for the partition, not just the crash: crashed nodes stay dead; partitioned nodes keep running and diverge. Tests should partition networks (iptables), not just kill processes.

lessons.title: Races and Shared State
concepts: A data race: two threads access the same memory, at least one writes, no synchronization. The result depends on timing — the definition of a Heisenbug.
Shared mutable state is the root of all concurrency evil: every race, deadlock, and visibility bug traces to it. Minimize it (immutable data, message passing, thread-local) and most bugs vanish.
Visibility is separate from atomicity: one thread's write may never become visible to another without a memory barrier (volatile/atomic/lock). 'It worked on x86' is not a correctness argument.
Reproduce races with stress + sanitizers: ThreadSanitizer finds races deterministically-ish; loop tests 10k times. 'Cannot reproduce' means 'have not stressed enough.'

lessons.title: Locks and Deadlocks
concepts: Mutexes serialize access to critical sections: lock, touch shared state, unlock. Hold them for the shortest time possible — locks are a concurrency tax.
Deadlock's four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait): break any one. In practice: global lock ordering (always acquire A before B) breaks circular wait.
Lock granularity is the tuning knob: one big lock (simple, serializes everything) vs fine-grained (complex, more parallelism). Start coarse, split only the contended ones.
Try-lock with timeout converts deadlocks into errors: if you cannot acquire in T ms, back off and retry. Deadlock becomes a recoverable failure instead of a hang.

lessons.title: Lock-Free and Atomics
concepts: Atomics (compare-and-swap) build lock-free structures: retry the CAS loop on contention. No deadlock, no priority inversion — but subtle and hard to prove correct.
Lock-free ≠ wait-free ≠ fast: lock-free guarantees system progress; a single thread can still starve. And CAS retries under heavy contention can be slower than a mutex.
Use lock-free for the hot paths experts profile: counters, queues (MPSC), read-mostly maps. For everything else, a mutex is clearer and fast enough — clarity beats cleverness.
Memory ordering matters: acquire/release semantics are usually sufficient; sequential consistency is the safe default. Get this wrong and the bug appears once a year on ARM.

lessons.title: Threads vs Async
concepts: Threads: one stack per task, blocking calls are fine, OS-scheduled. Best for CPU-bound work and when blocking libraries are unavoidable.
Async (event loop): one thread, many tasks, non-blocking I/O. Best for I/O-bound with massive concurrency (10k connections) — no per-thread stack overhead.
Never mix blocking calls into async: one blocking DB call stalls the entire event loop. Use thread pools for the blocking bits (run_in_executor) or async-native drivers.
Structured concurrency (task groups, nurseries) fixes async's cancellation chaos: child tasks are bound to a scope and cancelled together. Unstructured fire-and-forget is how tasks leak.

lessons.title: Parallel Patterns
concepts: Worker pools: fixed workers pull from a queue. The default for CPU-bound parallelism — bounded, backpressured, simple. Size to cores (CPU) or higher (I/O).
Map-reduce: map (parallel, no coordination) → shuffle → reduce. The pattern behind data-parallel frameworks; works when the problem partitions cleanly.
Pipeline parallelism: stages connected by queues (read → parse → transform → write). Each stage scales independently; the slowest stage sets throughput — find it and fix it.
Amdahl's law: speedup is limited by the serial fraction. 10% serial code caps you at 10x no matter the core count. Profile before parallelizing; parallelize the bottleneck.

lessons.title: Hypervisors
concepts: Type 1 (bare metal: KVM, Hyper-V, ESXi) runs on hardware; Type 2 (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) runs on an OS. Production is Type 1 — Type 2 is for laptops.
Hardware virtualization extensions (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) let guests run privileged instructions safely: near-native CPU speed. Without them, emulation crawls.
Overcommit: hypervisors can allocate more vCPU/RAM than physical (most VMs idle). Overcommit ratios are a capacity plan — exceed them and everyone slows together.
Snapshots are not backups: they depend on the base disk and grow on write. Great for pre-change rollback points; terrible as a retention strategy.

lessons.title: VMs vs Containers
concepts: VMs virtualize hardware (full guest OS per VM): strong isolation, minutes to boot, GBs each. Containers virtualize the OS (shared kernel): weak-er isolation, ms to start, MBs each.
Isolation strength differs: VM escape is rare; container escape (kernel vulnerability) affects all containers on the host. Match isolation to trust: untrusted tenants get VMs (or Kata/Firecracker).
Density differs 10-50x: a host runs dozens of VMs or thousands of containers. That density is why microservices are containers — and why noisy neighbors need limits.
The choice is a spectrum, not a war: VMs for strong isolation and odd OSes, containers for density and speed, and VM-isolated containers (Firecracker) when you want both.

lessons.title: Namespaces and Cgroups
concepts: Namespaces isolate what a process sees: PID, network, mount, UTS (hostname), IPC, user. A container is just a process with 6-7 namespaces applied.
Cgroups limit what a process uses: CPU shares/quota, memory limits, I/O weight, pids. The OOMKilled container died by cgroup limit — namespaces isolate, cgroups constrain.
You can build a 'container' by hand: unshare namespaces, set cgroup limits, chroot the filesystem. Doing it once demystifies everything Docker does.
User namespaces map container-root to unprivileged host UID: root in the container is nobody outside. The single biggest container-hardening lever — enable it.

lessons.title: Images and Registries
concepts: Images are stacked read-only layers: each Dockerfile instruction adds a layer. Layer caching makes rebuilds fast; layer bloat (apt caches, build tools) makes pulls slow.
Immutability: tag images by digest (sha256:...), not by 'latest.' 'Latest' is a moving target that makes rollbacks and audits impossible.
Multi-stage builds: compile in a fat builder image, copy artifacts into a slim runtime. The difference between a 1.2GB and a 40MB image — faster pulls, smaller attack surface.
Scan images in CI: base-image CVEs are your CVEs. Pin base images, rebuild regularly, and fail the build on critical vulnerabilities you actually expose.

lessons.title: Profiling

Invalidation is the hard part: TTLs (simple, stale-by-design), write-through (consistent, slower writes), event-driven invalidation (precise, complex). Pick by staleness tolerance.

lessons.title: Queues and Backpressure
concepts: Little's law: concurrency = throughput × latency. If latency doubles at fixed throughput, concurrency doubles — queues grow, memory grows, timeouts cascade.
Bounded queues with explicit overflow policy (drop oldest, drop newest, reject with 503): unbounded queues are memory leaks that accept traffic.
Backpressure propagates slowness upstream instead of collapsing: the fast producer must slow to the slow consumer's pace. Without it, buffers grow until OOM.
Load shedding: when overloaded, fail fast on low-priority work to protect the core. A system that sheds gracefully degrades; one that does not, dies.

Connection pooling and keepalive: handshake costs dominate short requests. Reuse connections; the setup cost amortizes to zero.
Know when to stop: the last 10% costs 90% of the effort. Optimize to the SLO with margin, then stop — perfect is the enemy of shipped.

lessons.title: SLOs and Error Budgets

Error budgets convert the SLO into a spendable allowance: 99.9% = 43 min/month of downtime. Spend it on deploys and experiments; freeze when it is gone.
SLIs are the measurements (success rate, latency); SLOs are the targets. Measure SLIs from the user's perspective (client-side), not the server's logs.
Burn-rate alerting: alert on how fast the budget burns, not on raw errors. Fast burn = page now; slow burn = ticket. Error budgets make alerting rational.

simulations.title: The full disk at 3 AM
simulations.brief: 3 AM page: the database server's disk is at 100% and writes are failing. The database will not start. Work it like an SRE.

steps.symptom: Disk at 100%. Database down. The obvious suspect is the log directory, but 'obvious' has burned you before.
evidence:
db-primary: disk 100% | postgres: will not start
Uptime: 214 days | last cleanup: unknown
options: Delete the oldest log files immediately to free space
Find what is actually consuming the space first — then delete with knowledge, not hope
Add a bigger disk and go back to sleep
Restart the database and hope it compacts
steps.explain: Deleting before measuring is how you delete the wrong thing at 3 AM. Find the consumers (logs? WAL? a runaway temp file?), then act. A bigger disk without understanding just postpones the next 3 AM page.

steps.symptom: Found it: 400 GB of uncompressed WAL archives from a backup job that broke 6 months ago — plus the actual logs are fine.
evidence:
/var/lib/postgres/wal_archive: 400 GB (6 months, uncompressed)
Backup job: broken since April | logs: 12 GB (normal)
options: Delete all 400 GB now
Verify the archives are truly unneeded (no replica depends on them, backups exist elsewhere), compress or move a sample first, then clear with a documented command
Compress them in place and leave them
Leave them — disk is cheap, just add more
steps.explain: Even obvious junk gets verified before deletion: a replica replaying WAL would die if you nuke its archives. Check dependencies, move before you delete when you can, and document the command — 3 AM you is not to be trusted with rm -rf.

steps.symptom: Space freed, database up. Now make sure no human gets this page again.
options: Set a disk alert at 95%
Fix the broken backup job, add log rotation with retention policy, alert at 80% with a runbook link, and trend disk growth on a dashboard
Schedule a monthly manual cleanup
Buy bigger disks for all servers
steps.explain: Alerting at 95% pages a human for a problem that started months ago. The real fixes: repair the backup job (the source), rotate logs with retention (the policy), alert at 80% (the lead time), trend the growth (the foresight). Pages should be for surprises, not slow inevitabilities.

simulations.debrief: You measured before deleting, verified before purging, and fixed the source instead of the symptom. Disk-full is never about disk — it is about the process that let it fill.

simulations.title: Split brain
simulations.brief: A network partition split your cluster: both halves think they are primary, both are taking writes. The partition just healed. Decide how to reconcile two divergent truths.

steps.symptom: Partition lasted 40 minutes. Side A took 12,000 writes; side B took 8,000 writes. Both believed they were primary.
evidence:
Partition: 40 min | A: 12,000 writes | B: 8,000 writes
Both sides: believed primary | conflict rate: unknown
options: Keep side A (more writes) and discard side B
Stop writes, measure the actual conflicts (same keys touched on both sides), then reconcile by rule — last-write-wins is a policy decision, not a default
Merge everything — writes are writes
Pick side B; fewer writes means less to reconcile
steps.explain: More writes does not mean more correct — it means more to lose. You freeze writes first (stop the divergence growing), measure real conflicts key by key, then apply a deliberate reconciliation policy. 'Most writes wins' is how you silently corrupt data.

steps.symptom: Conflict analysis: 3% of keys were written on both sides. The rest are disjoint.
evidence:
Disjoint keys: 97% (safe to merge)
Conflicting keys: 3% (~600 keys)
Of conflicts: 80% are counters, 20% are user records
options: Apply last-write-wins to everything
Merge the disjoint 97% automatically; resolve counters with CRDT-style addition and hand the 120 user-record conflicts to the owning teams with both versions
Discard all of side B's conflicting keys
Ask the CEO to decide
steps.explain: Different data types get different reconciliation: disjoint keys merge safely, counters add (order does not matter for increments), and true user-record conflicts need human judgment with both versions visible. One rule for all data types is how reconciliation creates new corruption.

steps.symptom: Reconciled. Now prevent the next split-brain.
evidence: Team: 'How do we never do this again?'
options: Add more nodes to each side
Require a quorum for primary election (no majority, no primary), add fencing so a deposed primary cannot keep writing, and test partitions in game days
Get a better network
Run everything on one big server
steps.explain: Split-brain is prevented by consensus mechanics, not hope: quorum means a minority partition cannot elect itself primary, fencing means the old primary gets shot before it writes, and game days prove it works. Partitions are inevitable; dual primaries are a choice.

simulations.debrief: You froze the divergence, reconciled by data type, and installed quorum plus fencing. Distributed systems do not avoid partitions — they decide in advance what happens during them.

simulations.title: The slow query vs the slow network
simulations.brief: The app is slow. The database team blames the network; the network team blames the database. You have one hour and a packet capture. Settle it.

steps.symptom: P99 request time tripled overnight. DB team: 'network latency.' Network team: 'slow queries.' Both have graphs.
evidence:
DB team graph: query times normal (their sampling: 1%)
Network team graph: no packet loss (their window: 5-min avg)
Reality: users see 3x slowdown
options: Pick a side based on who argues better
Measure the layers independently: time the query at the database, time the network round-trip separately, and see which one actually moved
Restart both the database and the routers
Add caching to hide it
steps.explain: Blame tennis ends with independent measurement: query time measured AT the database versus network time measured WITHOUT the query. Each team's graph was technically true and practically useless — 1% sampling and 5-minute averages both hide the thing you are looking for.

steps.symptom: Measured: queries are fast at the database (20ms), but the app-to-DB round trip is 400ms. The network is clean — no loss, no congestion.
evidence:
Query at DB: 20ms | app-to-DB round trip: 400ms
Network: 0% loss, no congestion
Gap: 380ms unexplained
options: Blame the network team anyway
Look between the layers: connection pool exhaustion, DNS resolution per query, or TLS handshake per connection — the gap lives in the plumbing, not the wire
Accept 400ms as normal
Move the database next to the app
steps.explain: Fast queries plus a clean network with a slow round trip means the overhead is in the plumbing: exhausted pools queueing, DNS lookups per query, handshakes per connection. The layers are not just 'app, network, DB' — the middleware between them has its own physics.

steps.symptom: Found: the connection pool was sized for the old traffic, and DNS was resolving on every checkout. Fixed both. What do you institutionalize?
evidence: Pool resized | DNS cached | round trip: 400ms -> 35ms
options: Nothing — it is fixed
Add layered latency breakdown to the standard dashboard (app, pool wait, network, query) so the next slowdown arrives pre-diagnosed
Write a postmortem blaming the pool defaults
Double all pool sizes everywhere preemptively
steps.explain: The lasting fix is observability shaped like the system: a latency breakdown by layer means the next incident starts with the answer instead of the argument. Diagnose once, instrument forever.

simulations.debrief: You refused the blame tennis, measured each layer independently, found the plumbing overhead, and dashboarded the breakdown. Slow systems are layered — measure the layers.

simulations.title: Thundering herd on deploy
simulations.brief: The deploy restarted all 200 instances at once. Every instance is cold-starting, hammering the database and the config service simultaneously. The site is flapping. Respond.

steps.symptom: All 200 instances restarted in the same minute. Config service is melting; database connections are exhausted; the site flaps up and down.
evidence:
200/200 instances restarted simultaneously
Config service: overloaded | DB: connection exhaustion
Site: flapping
options: Restart everything again — maybe it will settle
Stop the bleeding: halt the rollout, let the config service and DB recover, then bring instances up in small batches with health gates
Add more database connections
Wait for the herd to finish
steps.explain: A thundering herd gets worse before it gets better if you let it run: every retry joins the stampede. Halt, let the dependencies breathe, then reintroduce load in batches with health gates. Recovery is sequenced, not simultaneous.

steps.symptom: Batched restart worked — site is stable. The team wants to deploy the same way next time but 'more carefully.'
evidence: Team: 'We'll just watch it more closely next time.'
options: Agree — vigilance is enough
Change the deploy mechanics: rolling restarts with a batch size and health gates, so a herd is structurally impossible — not just watched for
Deploy at 3 AM when nobody notices
Halve the instance count
steps.explain: 'Watch more carefully' is not a fix — it is a hope with a human attached. Rolling deploys with batch sizes and health gates make the herd impossible by construction. Vigilance does not scale; mechanics do.

steps.symptom: Rolling deploys are in. What about the cold-start storm itself — 200 instances still need config and DB connections eventually?
evidence: Rolling deploys spread the load, but each instance still cold-starts hard
options: Accept it — rolling is enough
Soften the cold start too: staggered jitter on startup, cached config with graceful fallback, and connection ramp-up instead of instant full pools
Pre-warm by deploying twice
Overprovision everything 3x
steps.explain: Defense in depth for startup: rolling spreads the herd, jitter desynchronizes it, cached config removes a dependency, and ramped connections protect the database. Each layer is cheap; together they make cold starts boring.

simulations.debrief: You halted the stampede, made herds structurally impossible, and softened the cold start itself. Distributed systems fail in coordinated ways — so you coordinate the recovery.

simulations.title: To cache or not
simulations.brief: The product page loads in 800ms; the database groans. A cache would cut it to 50ms — but prices change, and stale prices mean angry customers and refunds. Decide.

steps.symptom: Page load: 800ms, DB at 70% on peak. Cache proposal: 50ms loads, 5-minute TTL on product data including prices.
evidence:
Without cache: 800ms, DB 70% peak
With cache (5-min TTL): 50ms, DB 20%
Risk: price changes visible up to 5 min late
options: Cache everything for 5 minutes — speed wins
Split by data type: cache the slow-changing catalog aggressively, keep prices on a short TTL or write-through invalidation — freshness follows the cost of staleness
Do not cache — correctness first
Cache for 24 hours — maximum speed
steps.explain: Caching is a per-data-type decision driven by the cost of staleness: a stale product description annoys; a stale price costs refunds and trust. Cache the catalog hard, keep prices fresh with short TTLs or invalidation on write. One TTL for everything is how you get the worst of both.

steps.symptom: Split caching approved. Now: what happens when the cache itself fails?
evidence: Cache cluster: single region, no failover tested
options: Accept the risk — caches rarely fail
Design for cache failure: the app must work (slower) with the cache down — cache-aside with DB fallback, never cache-as-requirement
Buy a bigger cache cluster
Replicate the cache to three regions
steps.explain: A cache is a performance optimization, not a dependency: the system must degrade to 'slow but correct' when it dies. Cache-aside with database fallback means a cache outage is a latency incident, not a data incident.

steps.symptom: Cache is live: 50ms loads, prices fresh, fallback tested. What do you watch?
options: Hit rate only
Hit rate, stale-serve incidents, invalidation lag, and fallback frequency — the cache's health is measured in correctness, not just speed
Nothing — it works
Page load time only
steps.explain: Cache monitoring is correctness monitoring: hit rate tells you it is helping, invalidation lag tells you it is fresh, fallback frequency tells you it is fragile. A fast cache serving stale prices is a fast way to lose money.

simulations.debrief: You split caching by staleness cost, designed for cache failure, and monitored correctness over speed. Caching is easy; cache invalidation and failure modes are the actual engineering.

consoleSims.title: Lock down the app config
consoleSims.brief: The app config at /etc/app.conf is world-readable (644) — it contains secrets. Restrict it to owner-only access with chmod 600.
consoleSims.debrief: Config with secrets gets 600: the owner reads it, nobody else does. Permissions are the cheapest security control you own.

consoleSims.title: Stage the backup directory
consoleSims.brief: The backup plan needs a home. Create the directory /home/user/backups, then create a README file inside it documenting the plan.
consoleSims.debrief: Backups start with a place to put them and a README saying what goes there. Boring, deliberate, recoverable.

consoleSims.title: Segment the server VLAN
consoleSims.brief: The servers need their own broadcast domain. Create VLAN 20 named 'servers', assign port gi0/5 to it as an access port, then save the config — unsaved configs evaporate on reboot.

tasks.hint: In the CLI box type: vlan 20 name servers

tasks.instruction: Assign port gi0/5 to VLAN 20 as an access port.
tasks.hint: In the CLI box type: interface gi0/5 access vlan 20
In the CLI box type: write memory

consoleSims.debrief: Segment, assign, save. The unsaved config is the classic outage: everything works until the reboot.

consoleSims.title: Deploy the API to prod
consoleSims.brief: Ship the API: create the prod namespace, deploy api (image api:2.14, 3 replicas) into it, then expose it as a ClusterIP service on port 80.

tasks.instruction: Deploy 'api' (image api:2.14, 3 replicas) into the prod namespace.
Expose the api deployment on port 80 as a ClusterIP service.

consoleSims.debrief: Namespace, deploy, expose: the shipping loop. Namespaces are cheap isolation — prod gets its own.

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
